title: Emergence and Recovery of (logical) Kochen-Specker Contextuality via Hamilton Extension
authors: Jayashree Karmakar, Biswadeep Chatterjee, Rafiuddin Gazi, Anushko Chattopadhyay, Ananya Chakraborty, Snehasish Roy Chowdhury, Amit Mukherjee, Manik Banik
abstract: Logical Kochen-Specker (KS) contextuality is widely regarded as an intrinsic property of specially constructed measurement configurations. We show instead that it can emerge from KS-colorable vector sets through a constructive procedure we call the Hamilton extension. Defined for four-dimensional vector sets, the Hamilton extension associates each real vector with a measurement context while inducing additional measurement contexts among Hamilton-extended children of distinct parent vectors. These emergent contexts fundamentally alter the compatibility structure, transforming KS-colorable configurations into KS-uncolorable ones and recovering logical contextuality lost under apex-vertex augmentation. We establish a sharp and optimal threshold -- the Hamilton extension of every five-vector parent set remains KS-colorable, whereas suitably chosen six-vector parent sets already generate logical KS contradictions. Thus, six vectors constitute the smallest parent set capable of generating KS contradiction through this mechanism. Our results reveal a new structural route to contextuality, provide a systematic framework for constructing compact KS sets, and have implications for contextuality-based quantum information protocols and graph-theoretic approaches to nonclassicality.
summary: This paper introduces the Hamilton extension as a method to systematically generate and recover logical Kochen-Specker contextuality in quantum systems. By analyzing how this construction transforms vector sets, the authors establish that six vectors constitute the smallest set capable of generating a contradiction with noncontextual hidden variables. This offers a new structural route for understanding fundamental limitations on quantum theories.
main_problem: The research investigates how logical Kochen-Specker (KS) contextuality, a hallmark of quantum mechanics, can emerge from mathematically structured vector sets rather than just being observed in specific configurations.
main_result: A constructive procedure called the Hamilton extension is shown to generate logical KS contradictions when applied to six or more parent vectors, establishing six as the minimum size required for this emergence.
method: The authors employ the Hamilton extension, a construction based on quaternion algebra, to augment vector sets and analyze the resulting orthogonality graphs using graph coloring arguments related to KS colorings.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum measurements represented by vector sets in $\mathbb{R}^4$ or $\mathbb{C}^d$, analyzed through their associated orthogonality graphs. The core mathematical tool is the Hamilton extension, $H[V]$.
key_observables: Logical Kochen-Specker contextuality (non-colorability of the derived graph structure) and the existence/structure of emergent measurement contexts.
important_parameters: The minimum parent set cardinality required to generate contradiction is six vectors. The analysis distinguishes between five-vector sets (always colorable) and six-vector sets (can be uncolorable).
main_assumptions: The proof for the threshold relies on exhaustive case analysis of emergent contexts generated by five Hamilton-distinct projectors, showing they are always KS-colorable.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate apex augmentation effects and the structure of Hamiltonian extensions ($H[V]$), detailing how parent vectors generate 'Hamilton contexts' and additional edges create 'emergent contexts.'
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the Hamilton extension, then demonstrating its ability to recover contextuality lost via apex augmentation. It establishes a sharp threshold theorem regarding the minimum size of the parent set required for contradiction (six vectors). Finally, it provides detailed proofs showing that five-vector sets are always colorable while specific six-vector sets yield contradictions.
why_interesting: The work provides a systematic, constructive framework to engineer quantum nonclassicality using algebraic structures, which is highly relevant for theoretical understanding of contextuality beyond standard Bell tests.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (Color online) Illustration of apex augmentation and Hamilton extension. The cycle graph C5 (bottom left) admits an orthogonal representation in R3. Adding an apex vertex adjacent to all vertices of C5 yields the wheel graph W6 (top left), which admits an orthogonal representation in R4. The Hamilton extension H[W6] is shown on the right. Each parent vertex generates a Hamilton context, while additional edges give rise to emergent contexts, e.g. {⃗vB,⃗v2,⃗v9,⃗v11}.

Figure 2. (Color online) Hamilton extensions generating logical KS contextuality. Left: the extension H[V8] of Theorem 1, yielding a new 32-vector logical KS set in R4. Middle: the extension H[V6] of Theorem 2, which coincides with the Peres-24 [28]. Green, cyan, and red indicate Hamilton contexts, emergent contexts of Type (2-2), and emergent contexts of Type (1-1-1-1), respectively. The set P24 contains as subsets the KS constructions K20 [32] and C18 [33]. Right: 24-vector KS set H [V′ 6]. It contains 12 Type (1-1-1-1) and 6 Type (2-2) emergent contexts and structurally different than Peres-24 construction which contains 18 Type (2-2) emergent contexts; additional structural relations...

Figure 3. (Color online) Graphical representation of the inner-product relations between the elements of H[u] and H[v] for u, v ∈RP3. Each edge color labels a distinct inner-product value; edges sharing the same color represent equal inner products.

Figure 4. (Color online) Left: Orthogonality graph of the set YO14. The red vertex (top) is the apex vertex. The graph obtained by removing the apex admits an orthogonal representation in R3, while the full graph admits one only in R4. Right: Orthogonality graph of the set CN18. For both graphs, the classical chromatic number exceeds the corresponding quantum chromatic number [41, 47].
